title: The Sign of ΔG and not ΔG° Determines the Direction of Reaction Spontaneity
lead: The standard reaction Gibbs energy refers to every species at 1 bar or 1 M and unmixed, which no real reaction is. The synthesis of ammonia shows why the reaction Gibbs energy at the actual composition is the one that decides.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise and its solution are AI-written. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.source_id: do not actually represent real reaction conditions
exercises.prompt: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), $\kDeltarGstd = -32.9$ kJ/mol at 298.15 K. What is $\kDeltarG$ for a mixture with NH₃ at 1 bar and N₂ and H₂ at 0.010 bar each?

answer.hint: Find Q from the pressures in bar, then add RT ln Q to the standard value.
answer.solution: $Q = \dfrac{1^2}{(0.010)(0.010)^3} = 1.0\times10^{8}$, so $\kR\kT\ln Q = (8.314)(298.15)(18.42)\ \text{J/mol} = 45.7$ kJ/mol and $\kDeltarG = -32.9 + 45.7 = +12.8$ kJ/mol. Although $\kDeltarGstd < 0$, this mixture holds so little N₂ and H₂ that the reaction runs in reverse: NH₃ decomposes.

footnotes.html: The unit of $\Delta_rG^\circ = -32.9$ and of $\Delta_rG = 0$ is kJ/mol, not kJ/(mol K): a Gibbs energy of reaction carries no kelvin.
Read H₂: the reactants are N₂ and H₂, and no O₂ takes part.
